Non-Pipelined Execution Time 
Frequency (f) = 2 GHz 
Cycle Time (T) = 1 / 2 GHz = 0.5 nsec 
Cycles per Instruction (CPI) = 6 cycles 
Total Execution Time (ET_Nonpipe) 
= CPI * Cycle Time = 6 * 0.5 nsec = 3 nsec 
Pipelined Execution Time with Stalls 
Cycle time remains 0.5 nsec. 
Instruction breakdown based on stalls: 
20% of instructions cause 2 stalls (Data Hazards) 
20% of instructions cause 3 stalls (Control 
Hazards) 
60% of instructions execute normally with 0 stalls 
Average Stalls per Instruction 
= (0.20 * 2) + (0.20 * 3) + (0.60 * 0) 
Average Stalls = 0.4 + 0.6 = 1 stall per instruction 
Average Execution Time (ET_Pipe) = 
(1 + Average Stalls) * Cycle Time 
ET_Pipe = (1 + 1) * 0.5 nsec = 2 * 0.5 nsec 
= 1 nsec 
Speedup Calculation 
Speedup (S) = ET_Nonpipe / ET_Pipe 
S = 3 nsec / 1 nsec = 3

An instruction placed in a branch delay slot always 
executes, regardless of whether the branch is taken 
or not. To safely fill it with an instruction from before 
the branch, that instruction must have no data 
dependencies affecting the branch condition or 
subsequent logic. 
The branch condition depends entirely on register 𝑅1 
( if R1 == 0). 
 𝐼3 cannot be moved: It writes directly to 
𝑅1 ( ADD R1 +R2 + R3 ). Moving it below 
the branch means the branch would 
evaluate using an old, incorrect value of 
𝑅1.
 𝐼1 cannot be moved: It computes 𝑅2 
(ADD R2 + R7 + R8 ), which is 
needed immediately by 𝐼3 to 
compute the branch register 𝑅1. 
Moving it would break this critical 
data chain.
c. 𝐼2 cannot be moved: It computes 𝑅4 ( SUB R4 + R5 − 
R6 ), which is needed immediately by the memory 
write address in 𝐼4. 
d. 𝐼4 can be moved: It is a simple store instruction ( 
STORE Memory [R4] & R1). It reads 𝑅4 and 𝑅1 
but does not alter any registers that the branch relies 
on. All of its 
own source operands are fully calculated by the time the 
program reaches this block.

dbms-topic-6-m6-q34.explanation:
Explanation :- 
When a database system recovers from a crash 
using a log file, it classifies transactions into 
two categories based on their status at the time 
of the crash: 
1. Committed Transactions (REDO): If a 
transaction has both a <start> and a <commit> 
record in the log, its changes must be 
preserved. 
 Transaction T1 has a T1 commit (record 4) 
before the crash. Thus, T1 must be redone (log 
records 2 and 3) to ensure durability. 
2. Uncommitted Transactions (UNDO): If a 
transaction has a <start> record but lacks a 
<commit> record in the log, its changes must 
be rolled back to maintain atomicity and 
consistency. 
 Transaction T2 crashes before writing its 
commit record (record 7). Thus, T2 must be 
undone (log record 6) to revert any partial 
modifications. 
(a) Incorrect: Log record 6 belongs to T2. 
Since T2 did not commit, its changes cannot 
be redone. 
(b) Correct: To restore consistency, we roll 
back the uncommitted change from T2 
(undoing log record 6 to reset B to 10000) and 
re-apply the committed changes from T1 
(redoing log records 2 and 3). 
(c) Incorrect: Even though T1 committed, 
standard recovery requires redoing its log 
records to ensure those changes are safely 
written to the physical disk (durability). 
(d) Incorrect: Redo and undo operations 
cannot be applied in an arbitrary order; they 
must follow strict ordering (typically, undoing 
active transactions backward and redoing 
committed transactions forward) to avoid 
corrupting data states.

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
The portion of code that cannot be parallelized takes 
10 ns. 
For each additional core, an overhead of 10 ns is 
added. 
Thus, overhead for n cores = (n − 1) × 10 ns. 
The parallelizable portion takes 90 ns on one core. 
On n cores, it takes 90 / n ns. 
Let total execution time be t(n): 
t(n) = 10 + (n − 1) × 10 + 90 / n 
= 10n + 90 / n 
Now evaluating: 
t(1) = 10(1) + 90/1 = 100 ns 
t(2) = 20 + 45 = 65 ns 
t(3) = 30 + 30 = 60 ns 
t(4) = 40 + 22.5 = 62.5 ns 
t(5) = 50 + 18 = 68 ns 
Minimum execution time occurs at n = 3. 
Answer: 3 cores 
Alternate Solution: 
Single Core Setup 
Total execution time on a single core = 100 nsec 
Parallelizable portion (90%) = 90 nsec 
Non-parallelizable portion (10%) = 10 nsec 
Adding Cores and Overhead 
Let the total number of cores = n 
Number of newly added cores = (n - 1) 
Overhead time per new core = 10 nsec 
Total overhead time for new cores = (n - 1) * 10 nsec 
Execution Time (ET) Equation 
ET = (Parallelizable Time / n) + Total Overhead + Non-
parallelizable Time 
ET = [90 / n + (n - 1) * 10] + 10 
ET = 90 / n + 10n - 10 + 10 
ET = 90 / n + 10n 
Finding the Optimal Number of Cores (Minimizing ET) 
To find the minimum execution time 
(Maxima/Minima), take the derivative of ET with 
respect to n and set it to 0: 
<!-- PAGE 465 -->
Computer Organization and Architecture 
d(ET)/dn = 0 
d(ET)/dn = d/dn [90 / n + 10n] 
d(ET)/dn = -90 / n2 + 10 
Set the derivative to 0: 
-90 / n2 + 10 = 0 
10 = 90 / n2 
10n2 = 90 
n2 = 9 
n = 3

Note that Empty String ϵ is Not accepted by the given PDA, 
So options B, C, D are eliminated. 
Empty String ϵ is Not accepted because from initial state, on 
empty tape, we cannot empty our stack since stack bottom 
symbol ⟂ can be removed only in state q But on empty tape, 
we can not reach to state q from state s. 
Method 2: 
Note that to empty our stack, the stack bottom symbol ⟂ can 
be removed only in state q. To reach state q, from s or from 
p, we need symbol A on Top-of-the-stack (TOS). Symbol A 
is pushed in the stack by symbol a in the input string. So, 
our input string must have at least one a. 
In the initial state s, for every a in the input string, we push 
one A in the stack. Now, for every b in the input string, we 
pop one A from the stack. When all the b′s are over in the 
input string, we can move to state q if our TOS is A, so, to 
empty our stack at the end of any input string w, we must 
have more a′s than b′s in w. In the state q we can empty the 
stack & w is accepted. 
Also, our PDA accepts a+strings.

Alternate Solution: 
Finding the Stage Time Ratios 
Given equations: T1 = (3 * T2) / 4 = 2 * T3 
From T1 = (3 * T2) / 4, we get the ratio: T1 / T2 
= 3 / 4 (which is equivalent to 6 / 8) 
From (3 * T2) / 4 = 2 * T3, we get the ratio: T2 / T3 
= 8 / 3 
Combined ratio for the stages: T1 : T2 : T3 = 6 : 8 : 
Initial Pipeline Cycle Time 
Let 'x' be a constant unit of time. 
The stage times are: T1 = 6x, T2 = 8x, T3 = 3x 
The pipeline cycle time (tp) is the maximum of the 
stage times. 
tp = max(6x, 8x, 3x) 
tp = 8x 
Solving for Base Frequency 
Frequency = 1 / Cycle Time 
The given initial frequency is 3 GHz. 
3 GHz = 1 / 8x 
Solving for 1/x: 1 / x = 3 GHz * 8 = 24 GHz 
New Pipeline Design (Splitting the Bottleneck) 
The longest stage (8x) is split into two equal sub-
stages. 
8x becomes -> 4x and 4x 
The new sequence of stage times is: 6x, 4x, 4x, 3x 
New pipeline cycle time (tp_new) = max(6x, 4x, 4x, 
3x) 
tp_new = 6x 
Calculating the New Frequency 
New Frequency (Freq_new) = 1 / tp_new 
Freq_new = 1 / 6x 
We can rewrite this as: Freq_new = (1 / 6) * (1 / x) 
Substitute the value of (1 / x) we found earlier (24 
GHz): 
Freq_new = (1 / 6) * 24 GHz 
New Frequency = 4 GHz

This sequence performs a swap of A[i][j] and A[j][i].

of indices (i,j) from 1 to n. 
Net Effect:

loops process the pair twice: once as (i,j) and once as

A swap operation performed twice on the same pair of 
memory locations returns the elements to their original 
positions and values. 
For i=j (diagonal elements), the element is swapped 
with itself, resulting in no change. 
Final Output: Since the matrix A is restored to its 
initial state after the first set of loops, the second set of 
loops, which prints A[i][j] in row -major order, prints 
the original matrix A. 
Therefore, the expected output is The matrix A itself. 
The correct option is: The matrix A itself

The constant C=100 is added and then subtracted, 
having no net effect on the values themselves. 
Loop Structure: The nested loops iterate over all pairs 
of indices (i,j) from 1 to n. 
Net Effect: 
For any pair where i!=j (off -diagonal elements), the 
loops process the pair twice: once as (i,j) and once as 
(j,i). 
A swap operation performed twice on the same pair of 
memory locations returns the elements to their original 
positions and values. 
For i=j (diagonal elements), the element is swapped 
with itself, resulting in no change. 
Final Output: Since the matrix A is restored to its 
initial state after the first set of loops, the second set of 
loops, which prints A[i][j] in row -major order, prints 
the original matrix A. 
Therefore, the expected output is The matrix A itself. 
The correct option is: The matrix A itself

adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. Let's 
analyze how many swap operations are performed when

is 28 iterations.

runs only once.

of the first 29 numbers:

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
Base Pipeline Execution Time 
Instruction Sequence: ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, 
MUL, ADD, MUL 
EX Stage Cycles per instruction: ADD = 1, MUL = 2, 
ADD = 1, MUL = 2, ADD = 1, MUL = 2, ADD = 1, 
MUL = 2 
Number of Pipeline Stages (k) = 5 Stages 
Number of Instructions (n) = 8 Instructions 
Ideal Execution Time (ET_PIPE) = [k + (n - 1)] cycles 
<!-- PAGE 466 -->
Computer Organization and Architecture 
Ideal ET_PIPE = [5 + (8 - 1)] = 12 cycles 
Execution Time WITH Operand Forwarding 
Each ADD instruction takes 1 cycle in the EX stage. 
Each MUL instruction takes 2 cycles in the EX 
stage. 
Out of 8 instructions, 4 are MUL instructions. 
These 4 MUL instructions take 1 extra cycle each in 
the EX stage. 
Extra cycles = 4 instructions * 1 extra cycle = 4 
cycles 
Total ET (With Forwarding) = 12 (Base) + 4 (Extra 
EX cycles) = 16 cycles 
Execution Time WITHOUT Operand Forwarding 
Every instruction depends on the result of the 
previous instruction (Data dependency: ADD -> 
MUL -> ADD -> MUL ...). 
Without forwarding, each data dependency 
introduces a 2-cycle stall penalty. 
Out of 8 instructions, 7 instructions depend on the 
previous one, thus incurring the 2-cycle stall penalty. 
Total Stalls = 7 instructions * 2 stall cycles = 14 
cycles 
Total ET (Without Forwarding) = Total ET (With 
Forwarding) + Stall Cycles 
Total ET = 16 + 14 = 30 cycles 
Speedup Calculation 
Speedup = Total ET (Without Forwarding) / Total 
ET (With Forwarding) 
Speedup = 30 / 16 = 1.875

Deadlock Prevention:

four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-
and-wait, no preemption, circular wait).

check — it follows strict rules regardless of safety.

whether granting a request keeps the system in a safe 
state.

Hence, (B) is true. 
 Avoidance is less restrictive than prevention because 
it allows more flexibility → (C) is true.

resource needs → (D) is true.

Note that Empty String ϵ is Not accepted by the given PDA, 
So options B, C, D are eliminated. 
Empty String ϵ is Not accepted because from initial state, on 
empty tape, we cannot empty our stack since stack bottom 
symbol ⟂ can be removed only in state q But on empty tape, 
we can not reach to state q from state s. 
Method 2: 
Note that to empty our stack, the stack bottom symbol ⟂ can 
be removed only in state q. To reach state q, from s or from 
p, we need symbol A on Top-of-the-stack (TOS). Symbol A 
is pushed in the stack by symbol a in the input string. So, 
our input string must have at least one a. 
In the initial state s, for every a in the input string, we push 
one A in the stack. Now, for every b in the input string, we 
pop one A from the stack. When all the b′s are over in the 
input string, we can move to state q if our TOS is A, so, to 
empty our stack at the end of any input string w, we must 
have more a′s than b′s in w. In the state q we can empty the 
stack & w is accepted. 
Also, our PDA accepts a+strings.

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
First, determine the clock cycle time of the pipeline. 
In an ideal pipeline, the clock cycle time is given by 
the delay of the slowest stage plus the inter-stage latch 
delay. 
Stage delays: 
Stage 1 = 180 ns 
Stage 2 = 250 ns 
Stage 3 = 150 ns 
Stage 4 = 170 ns 
Stage 5 = 250 ns 
Maximum stage delay = 250 ns 
Including  the  latch  delay  (10  ns): 
Clock cycle time (t_cycle) = 250 ns + 10 ns = 260 ns 
Next, consider the execution of 1000 instructions. For 
a pipeline with 5 stages, the first instruction requires 
5 cycles to complete, and each subsequent instruction 
completes in one additional cycle. 
Total number of cycles = n + (k − 1) 
= 1000 + (5 − 1) 
= 1000 + 4 
= 1004 cycles 
Now, calculate the total execution time: 
Total time = 1004 × 260 ns = 261040 ns 
Convert nanoseconds to microseconds: 
261040 ns = 261040 / 1000 = 261.04 μs 
Therefore, the total time required to process 1000 
instructions. is 261.04 microseconds.

The solution is using a binary semaphore. X and Y 
are two different processes, whatever the values 
inserted by the processes in the array that will be used 
by process Y afterwards. 
 A. X is waiting on R and Y is waiting on X. So, both 
cannot proceed. 
 B. Process  X is doing Signal  operation 
on R and S without any wait and hence multiple 
signal operations can happen on the binary semaphore 
so Process Y won't be able to get exactly n successful 
wait operations. i.e., Process  Y may not be able to 
complete all the iterations.  
<!-- PAGE 328 -->
OPERATING SYSTEMS 
 C. Process X does Wait(S) followed by Signal(R) 
while Process  Y does Signal(S) followed by 
Wait(R). So, this ensures that no two iterations of 
either XX or YY can proceed without an iteration 
of the other being executed in between. i.e., this 
ensures that all  n iterations of  X and Y succeeds 
and hence the answer.  
 D. Process X does Signal(R) followed by Wait(S) 
while Process  Y does Signal(S) followed by 
Wait(R). There is a problem here that X can do two 
Signal(R) operation without a Wait(R) being done 
in between by Y. This happens in the following 
scenario: 
 Process Y: Does Signal (S); Wait(R) fails; goes to 
sleep. 
 Process X: does Signal(R); Wait(S) succeeds; In 
next iteration Signal(R) again happens; 
 So, this can result in some Signal operations getting 
lost as  the semaphore is a binary one and thus 
Process Y may not be able to complete all the 
iterations. If we change the order of Signal(S) and 
Wait(R) in EntryY, then (D) option also can work.

theory-of-computation-topic-3-m3-q10.explanation:
The correct option is (a) 𝑓 is computable if and only if 𝐿𝑓 is 
recursive. 
Here is the step by step mathematical proof for both 
directions of the "if and only if" statement: 
Direction 1: If 𝑓 is computable, then 𝐿𝑓 is recursive ( ⇌ ) 
If 𝑓 is a computable total function, there exists a Tu ring 
machine 𝑀𝑓 that, when given an input 𝑥, is guaranteed to halt 
and leave 𝑓(𝑥) on its tape. We can construct a new decider 
Turing machine 𝑀𝐿 to decide the language 𝐿𝑓 = {𝑥# ∫  (𝑥) ∣
𝑥 ∈ 𝐴∗} as follows: 
1. Parse the input: Given an arbitrary input string 𝑤, 
check if it contains exactly one # symbol. If it 
doesn't, reject. 
2. Split the components: If it matches the format, 
split the string into the portion before the delimiter 
( 𝑥 ) and the portion after the delimiter ( 𝑦 ). So, 
𝑤 = 𝑥#𝑦. 
3. Simulate the funct ion: Run the computable 
machine 𝑀𝑓 on the input substring 𝑥. Because 𝑓 is 
a total computable function, 𝑀𝑓 is guaranteed to 
halt and output 𝑓(𝑥). 
4. Compare results: Compare the output 𝑓(𝑥) with 
the string 𝑦 from the input tape. 
 If 𝑓(𝑥) == 𝑦, then accept. 
 If 𝑓(𝑥) ≠ 𝑦, then reject. 
Since 𝑀𝑓 always halts, 𝑀𝐿 is guaranteed to always halt and 
make a definitive decision for any input string. Therefore, 𝐿𝑓 
is a recursive (decidable) language. 
Direction 2: If 𝐿𝑓 is recursive, then 𝑓 is computable ( ⇐ ) 
If 𝐿𝑓 is recursive, there exists a decider Turing machine 𝑀𝐿 
that can always determine whether a string of the form 𝑥#𝑦 
belongs to 𝐿𝑓 or not. We can construct a Turing machine 
𝑀𝑓 to compute the function 𝑓(𝑥) for any given i nput 𝑥 ∈
𝐴∗ : 
1. Generate candidate strings: Since the alphabet 𝐵 is finite, we 
can systematically generate all possible strings over 𝐵∗ 
in lexicographical order: 𝜖, 𝑏1, 𝑏2, … 
2. Test each candidate: For each generated string 𝑦 ∈ 𝐵∗, 
construct the combined string 𝑥#𝑦. 
3. Run the decider: Feed the string 𝑥#𝑦 into the decider 𝑀𝐿. 
 Since 𝑀𝐿 is a decider, it will always halt and either accept 
or reject. 
 If 𝑀𝐿 rejects, move to the next lexicographical string in 𝐵∗. 
 If 𝑀𝐿 accepts, it means 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑥). Stop the search, clear 
the tape, leave 𝑦 on the tape, and halt. 
Because 𝑓 is a total function, a valid output string 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑥) is 
guaranteed to exist somewhere in the lexicographical 
enumeration. Thus, 𝑀𝑓 will eventually find it, output it, and halt. 
This proves that 𝑓 is computable.

theory-of-computation-topic-2-m2-q4.explanation:
1. Is L(G1) = L(G2)? 
Undecidable. Determining if two context-free grammars 
(CFGs) generate the same language is undecidable. 
There is no algorithm that can decide whether two 
arbitrary CFGs generate the same language. 
2. Is L(G1) ∩ L(G2) = ∅? 
Undecidable. The intersection of two context -free 
languages is not necessarily context-free, and checking if 
two context-free languages have an empty intersection is 
undecidable. This is a generalization of the 
undecidability of the equivalence problem for CFGs. 
3. Is L(G1) = L(R)? 
Undecidable. The equivalence of a context-free language 
(generated by a CFG) and a regular language (defined by 
a regular expression) is undecidable. Determining 
whether a CFG generates a language that is exactly the 
same as a regular language is undecidable. 
4. Is L(G1) = ∅? 
Decidable. It is decidable whether the language 
generated by a context -free grammar G1 is empty. This 
can be determined by analyzing the grammar to check if 
there exists a derivation for any string. Specifically, this 
can be done by checking if there is any derivation starting 
from the start symbol and reaching a terminal string.

during addition if and only if two numbers

the resulting sum.

but the output sign bit is 0 . 
Condition 1 = 𝑎𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑏𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑐𝑛−1 
2. Adding two positive numbers yields a

Combining both mutually exclusive 
scenarios using an OR operation gives the

 Overflow = 𝑎𝑛−1𝑏𝑛−1𝑐𝑛−1 + 𝑎𝑛−1𝑏𝑛−1𝑐𝑛−1

graph cannot have multiple minimum

Explanation: 
In a singly linked list (SLL), each node has only a 
pointer to the next node. If we are given a pointer 
to the node to delete, we still need to know its 
previous node to change the link (prev->next = 
node->next). Since there is no backward pointer, 
we must traverse the list from the head to find the 
previous node. In the worst case, this takes O(n) 
time. 
In a doubly linked list (DLL), each node has 
pointers to both next and previous nodes. So, if we 
are given the node to delete, we can directly 
access its previous node and adjust links (prev- 
>next and 
next->prev) without any traversal. This takes O(1) 
time.

Explanation: 
Height = 6 means maximum possible height for 7 
nodes. 
So the BST must be completely skewed (a chain of 
7 nodes). 
Now think carefully. 
For height to be 6, at every step after choosing the 
root, all remaining elements must go only to one 
side (either all smaller or all greater). 
First, choose the root. 
If root is 1, then all remaining 6 elements (2–7) must 
go to the right side. 
If root is 7, then all remaining 6 elements (1–6) 
must go to the left side. 
If root is anything between 2 and 6, then some 
elements will go left and some right, so height will 
be less than 6. So only 1 or 7 can be the root. 
After fixing the root (say 1), the remaining 6 
elements must again form a skewed BST of height 5. 
So the problem reduces recursively. 
For 7 nodes to form a chain, at each step we must 
choose either the smallest or the largest element 
among the remaining elements. 
At first step: 2 choices (1 or 7). 
At second step: again 2 choices (smallest or largest 
of remaining 6). 
At third step: again 2 choices. 
This continues for 6 steps. 
Total ways = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 
= 2⁶ 
= 64

A. [β→(∃x α(x))]→[∀x (β→α(x))]  
 LHS: If β (some condition) is true, then there 
exists an x for which α(x) is true. 
 RHS: For all x, if β is true then α(x) is true. This is 
same as saying if β is true then for all x, α(x) is 
true. 
 (β ⇒ ∀x α(x)). 
 So, RHS ⇒ LHS and LHS ⇏ RHS. 
 B. [∃x (β→α(x))]→[β→(∀x α(x))] 
 LHS: There exists an x such that if β is true then 
α(x) is true. 
 RHS: If β is true then for all x, α(x) is true. 
 So, RHS ⇒ LHS and LHS ⇏ RHS. 
 C.[(∃x α(x))→β]→[∀x (α(x)→β)] 
 LHS: If there is an x such that α(x) is true, then β 
is true. 
 RHS: For all x, if α(x) is true, then β is true. 
 Here, both LHS and RHS are in fact same as β is a 
formula which is independent of x.(If β is true for 
one x, it is true for every x and vice versa.) 
 So,RHS ⇔ LHS. 
 D.[(∀x α(x))→β]→[∀x (α(x)→β)] 
 LHS: If α(x) is true for every x, then β is true. 
 RHS: For every x, if α(x) is true then β is true. 
 So, RHS ⇒ LHS and LHS ⇏ RHS. 
 So, answer here is option C. 
 Any of options A, B, or D could be valid if their 
implication is reversed. For option C, LHS and 
RHS being equivalent, even if the implication is 
reversed (or changed to double implies) it remains 
valid.

To calculate the average waiting time, we need to 
simulate the scheduling process step by step based 
on the given priorities and CPU bursts for the 
processes on processors M1 and M2. 
 Given Data: 
● Processor M1 Priority Order: P1 > P3 > P2 > P4 
● Processor M2 Priority Order: P2 > P3 > P4 > P1 
● CPU Bursts: 
o P1: 20 ms 
o P2: 16 ms 
o P3: 25 ms 
o P4: 10 ms 
 Process Scheduling on M1 and M2: 
1. Initial state: Both processors (M1 and M2) are 
free. 
2. Time 0: The scheduler starts with the highest 
priority processes based on each processor's 
priority list. 
● M1: The highest priority process is  P1 (with a 
burst of 20 ms), so P1 is allocated to M1. 
● M2: The highest priority process is  P2 (with a 
burst of 16 ms), so P2 is allocated to M2. 
1. After P1 finishes (at time 20 ms): 
o M1: The next highest priority process 
is P3 (with a burst of 25 ms), so  P3 is allocated 
to M1. 
o M2: P2 finishes at 16 ms, and the next 
highest priority process is  P3, but 
since M1 has already taken P3, M2 moves to 
the next highest priority, which is P4 (with a 
burst of 10 ms). 
2. After P2 finishes (at time 16 ms): 
o M1: P3 continues execution (since P3 is already 
allocated to M1). 
o M2: P4 finishes at time 26 ms, and now the 
remaining process is P3. 
 Calculate Waiting Times: 
● Waiting time is calculated as:  Waiting Time = 
Start Time - Arrival Time. 
 For Process P1: 
● P1 starts at time 0 and runs for 20 ms, so its 
waiting time is 0 ms. 
 For Process P2: 
● P2 starts at time 0 on M2 and runs for 16 ms. Its 
waiting time is 0 ms as it started at time 0. 
 For Process P3: 
● P3 starts at time 20 on M1 and runs for 25 ms. Its 
waiting time is  20 ms  (since it waited for  P1 to 
finish on M1). 
 For Process P4: 
● P4 starts at time 16 on M2 and runs for 10 ms. Its 
waiting ti me is  16 ms  (since it waited for  P2 to 
finish). 
 Average Waiting Time: 
 Now, we calculate the average waiting time: 
 P1: Waiting time = 0 ms 
 P2: Waiting time = 0 ms 
 P3: Waiting time = 20 ms 
 P4: Waiting time = 16 ms 
 Average waiting time = (0 + 0 + 20 + 16) / 4 = 36 / 4 
= 9.00 ms 
 Final Answer: 
 The average waiting time of the processes is 9.00 ms.

Page table base register:  This register stores the 
page table's base address for the currently executing 
thread. Because all threads in a process share the 
same page table, this register does not need to be 
saved. 
 Stack pointer: This register points to the top of the 
stack for the thread that is currently running. 
Because each thread has its own stack, the stack 
pointer must be saved and restored when the 
context changes to ensure that the new thread uses 
the correct stack. 
 PC: The address of the next instruction to be 
executed by the currently executing thread is stored 
in the program counter register. To restart the new 
thread, the saved program counter must be loaded 
into the program counter register. 
 General purpose registers : These registers are 
used to store temporary data and intermediate 
results during the execution of a thread.

Explanation: 
When you delete an arbitrary element at index ii 
in a binary heap: 
1. Swap the element at index ii with the last 
element in the heap. 
2. Remove the last element (now the original ii-th 
element). 
3. Heapify from index ii: 
○ May need to bubble up if it's larger than its 
parent (if it's a max-heap) 
○ Or bubble down if it's smaller than one of its 
children 
○ But since we don't know whether it's too large 
or too small, we must check both. 
However, in practice, we compare with parent: 
● If it's greater than parent (in max-heap), bubble 
up — O(d) 
● Else, bubble down — O(d) 
So in either case, we do at most one path up or 
down the tree. 
Height d = depth = O(log n) 
Thus time complexity = O(d)=O(log n) 
FINAL ANSWER = O(d)

Here is the step by step mathematical proof for both 
directions of the "if and only if" statement: 
Direction 1: If 𝑓 is computable, then 𝐿𝑓 is recursive ( ⇌ ) 
If 𝑓 is a computable total function, there exists a Tu ring 
machine 𝑀𝑓 that, when given an input 𝑥, is guaranteed to halt 
and leave 𝑓(𝑥) on its tape. We can construct a new decider 
Turing machine 𝑀𝐿 to decide the language 𝐿𝑓 = {𝑥# ∫  (𝑥) ∣
𝑥 ∈ 𝐴∗} as follows: 
1. Parse the input: Given an arbitrary input string 𝑤, 
check if it contains exactly one # symbol. If it 
doesn't, reject. 
2. Split the components: If it matches the format, 
split the string into the portion before the delimiter 
( 𝑥 ) and the portion after the delimiter ( 𝑦 ). So, 
𝑤 = 𝑥#𝑦. 
3. Simulate the funct ion: Run the computable 
machine 𝑀𝑓 on the input substring 𝑥. Because 𝑓 is 
a total computable function, 𝑀𝑓 is guaranteed to 
halt and output 𝑓(𝑥). 
4. Compare results: Compare the output 𝑓(𝑥) with 
the string 𝑦 from the input tape. 
 If 𝑓(𝑥) == 𝑦, then accept. 
 If 𝑓(𝑥) ≠ 𝑦, then reject. 
Since 𝑀𝑓 always halts, 𝑀𝐿 is guaranteed to always halt and 
make a definitive decision for any input string. Therefore, 𝐿𝑓 
is a recursive (decidable) language. 
Direction 2: If 𝐿𝑓 is recursive, then 𝑓 is computable ( ⇐ ) 
If 𝐿𝑓 is recursive, there exists a decider Turing machine 𝑀𝐿 
that can always determine whether a string of the form 𝑥#𝑦 
belongs to 𝐿𝑓 or not. We can construct a Turing machine 
𝑀𝑓 to compute the function 𝑓(𝑥) for any given i nput 𝑥 ∈
𝐴∗ : 
1. Generate candidate strings: Since the alphabet 𝐵 is finite, we 
can systematically generate all possible strings over 𝐵∗ 
in lexicographical order: 𝜖, 𝑏1, 𝑏2, … 
2. Test each candidate: For each generated string 𝑦 ∈ 𝐵∗, 
construct the combined string 𝑥#𝑦. 
3. Run the decider: Feed the string 𝑥#𝑦 into the decider 𝑀𝐿. 
 Since 𝑀𝐿 is a decider, it will always halt and either accept 
or reject. 
 If 𝑀𝐿 rejects, move to the next lexicographical string in 𝐵∗. 
 If 𝑀𝐿 accepts, it means 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑥). Stop the search, clear 
the tape, leave 𝑦 on the tape, and halt. 
Because 𝑓 is a total function, a valid output string 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑥) is 
guaranteed to exist somewhere in the lexicographical 
enumeration. Thus, 𝑀𝑓 will eventually find it, output it, and halt. 
This proves that 𝑓 is computable.

c-programming-topic-3-m3-q20.explanation:
Solution: 
For foo(3): 
In the statement foo(val--), the current value of val is 
passed to the function first and then it is decremented. 
So when val = 3, the function keeps calling foo(3) 
again before val decreases. 
Because of this, the recursive calls do not move 
towards termination. 
Hence, it leads to infinite recursion and finally stack 
overflow, i.e., abnormal termination. 
For bar(3): 
Inside the loop, the condition is while (val > 0) but 
val is never updated. 
Although the recursive call is bar(val - 1), the original 
val in the loop remains unchanged. 
So the loop condition always stays true. 
Hence, the function runs forever, resulting in an 
infinite loop. 
Therefore: 
foo(3) → Abnormal termination 
bar(3) → Infinite loop

Solution: 
To detect the faull, we should get an 
unexpected output. The final gate here is a 
NOR gate which produces output 0 if either of 
its input is 1 and else 1 , ie, the output will be 
0 for inputs (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1) and output 
will be 1 for (0,0). 
By grounding 𝑇 is at 0 . So, we can ignore the 
inputs (1,0) and (0,0) to the final NOR gate 
as they won't be detecting faults. Now, 
expected (1,1) input will become (1,0) due to 
grounding of 𝑇 but produces same output 0 as 
for (1,1). Hence this also cannot detect the 
defect. So, to detect the defect, the input to the 
final gate must be (0,1) which is expected to 
produce a 0 but will produce a 1 due to 
grounding of 𝑇. 
Now, for (0,1) input for the final gate, we 
must have, 
𝑋3 = 𝑋4 = 1 
But if 𝑋4 = 1,the OR gate makes 1 output 
and we won't get ( 0,1 ) input for the final 
gate. This means, no input sequence can 
detect the fault of the circuit. 
Alternatively, we can write equation for the 
circuit as 
(((𝑥1 ⋅ 𝑥2 ⋅ 𝑥3)′ + 𝑥4) + 𝑥3 ⋅ 𝑥4)′

For the faulty circuit output will be

1.  Early Resource Distribution (𝑡 = 0 to 𝑡 =
2) : All processes successfully grab their initial

𝑅1, which provides exactly what 𝑃3 needs to 
finish. 𝑃2 also finishes completely at 𝑡 = 8, 
releasing its remaining pool back to the 
system.

 L1 and L2 are recursive (decidable) because the 
condition is bounded by a fixed number of steps (2016). 
In 2016 steps, a Turing machine can read at most the 
first 2016 symbols on its tape. Because the alphabet is 
finite, there are a finite number of possible string prefixes 
of this length. A decider can simulate the machine on all 
these combinations for exactly 2016 steps. Since both 
the number of strings and the number of steps are finite, 
the simulation is guaranteed to halt and give an answer. 
 L3 is not recursive (undecidable) because checking 
whether a Turing machine accepts the empty string (ϵ) 
is the classic Blank Tape Acceptance Problem. 
According to Rice's Theorem, any non-trivial property 
about the language a Turing machine accepts cannot be 
decided by a general algorithm.

dbms-topic-6-m6-q34.explanation:
Explanation :- 
When a database system recovers from a crash 
using a log file, it classifies transactions into 
two categories based on their status at the time 
of the crash: 
1. Committed Transactions (REDO): If a 
transaction has both a <start> and a <commit> 
record in the log, its changes must be 
preserved. 
 Transaction T1 has a T1 commit (record 4) 
before the crash. Thus, T1 must be redone (log 
records 2 and 3) to ensure durability. 
2. Uncommitted Transactions (UNDO): If a 
transaction has a <start> record but lacks a 
<commit> record in the log, its changes must 
be rolled back to maintain atomicity and 
consistency. 
 Transaction T2 crashes before writing its 
commit record (record 7). Thus, T2 must be 
undone (log record 6) to revert any partial 
modifications. 
(a) Incorrect: Log record 6 belongs to T2. 
Since T2 did not commit, its changes cannot 
be redone. 
(b) Correct: To restore consistency, we roll 
back the uncommitted change from T2 
(undoing log record 6 to reset B to 10000) and 
re-apply the committed changes from T1 
(redoing log records 2 and 3). 
(c) Incorrect: Even though T1 committed, 
standard recovery requires redoing its log 
records to ensure those changes are safely 
written to the physical disk (durability). 
(d) Incorrect: Redo and undo operations 
cannot be applied in an arbitrary order; they 
must follow strict ordering (typically, undoing 
active transactions backward and redoing 
committed transactions forward) to avoid 
corrupting data states.

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
There are N accesses to cache. 
Out of these n are unique block addresses. 
Now, we need to find the number of misses. 
(Minimum n misses are guaranteed whatever be the 
access sequence due to n unique block addresses). 
We are given that between two consecutive accesses 
to the same block, there can be only k unique block 
addresses. So, for a block to get replaced we can 
assume that all the next k block addresses go to the 
same set (given cache is set-associative) which will 
be the worst case scenario (they may also go to a 
different set but then there is less chance of a 
replacement). Now, if associativity size ≥ k, and if 
we use LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement 
policy, we can guarantee that these k accesses won't 
throw out our previously accessed cache entry (for 
<!-- PAGE 516 -->
Computer Organization and Architecture 
that we need at least k accesses). So, this means 
we are at the best-cache scenario for cache 
replacement — out of N accesses we miss only n 
(which are unique and cannot be helped from 
getting missed and there is no block replacement 
in cache). So, the miss ratio is n/N.

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
The portion of code that cannot be parallelized takes 
10 ns. 
For each additional core, an overhead of 10 ns is 
added. 
Thus, overhead for n cores = (n − 1) × 10 ns. 
The parallelizable portion takes 90 ns on one core. 
On n cores, it takes 90 / n ns. 
Let total execution time be t(n): 
t(n) = 10 + (n − 1) × 10 + 90 / n 
= 10n + 90 / n 
Now evaluating: 
t(1) = 10(1) + 90/1 = 100 ns 
t(2) = 20 + 45 = 65 ns 
t(3) = 30 + 30 = 60 ns 
t(4) = 40 + 22.5 = 62.5 ns 
t(5) = 50 + 18 = 68 ns 
Minimum execution time occurs at n = 3. 
Answer: 3 cores 
Alternate Solution: 
Single Core Setup 
Total execution time on a single core = 100 nsec 
Parallelizable portion (90%) = 90 nsec 
Non-parallelizable portion (10%) = 10 nsec 
Adding Cores and Overhead 
Let the total number of cores = n 
Number of newly added cores = (n - 1) 
Overhead time per new core = 10 nsec 
Total overhead time for new cores = (n - 1) * 10 nsec 
Execution Time (ET) Equation 
ET = (Parallelizable Time / n) + Total Overhead + Non-
parallelizable Time 
ET = [90 / n + (n - 1) * 10] + 10 
ET = 90 / n + 10n - 10 + 10 
ET = 90 / n + 10n 
Finding the Optimal Number of Cores (Minimizing ET) 
To find the minimum execution time 
(Maxima/Minima), take the derivative of ET with 
respect to n and set it to 0: 
<!-- PAGE 465 -->
Computer Organization and Architecture 
d(ET)/dn = 0 
d(ET)/dn = d/dn [90 / n + 10n] 
d(ET)/dn = -90 / n2 + 10 
Set the derivative to 0: 
-90 / n2 + 10 = 0 
10 = 90 / n2 
10n2 = 90 
n2 = 9 
n = 3

Solution: 
Based on the given adjacency matrix: 
 Diagonal elements are 0: There are no self-
loops. 
 Non-diagonal elements are 1: There is an edge 
between every pair of distinct vertices, and every 
edge has a weight of 1. 
This describes a complete graph (Kn) where all 
edge weights are equal to 1. 
A spanning tree for a graph with n vertices must 
contain exactly n-1 edges. Since every edge in 
this graph has a weight of 1, the cost of any 
spanning tree will be exactly (n- 1)*1 = n-1. 
Because all edges have the exact same weight, 
any valid tree that connects all $n$ nodes is a 
Minimum Spanning Tree. According to Cayley's 
formula, a complete graph with n vertices has nn-
2 distinct spanning trees. As long as n > 2, there 
will be multiple distinct spanning trees. 
Therefore, there are multiple distinct MSTs, and 
every single one of them has a cost of n-1. 
The correct answer is C.

Note that Empty String ϵ is Not accepted by the given PDA, 
So options B, C, D are eliminated. 
Empty String ϵ is Not accepted because from initial state, on 
empty tape, we cannot empty our stack since stack bottom 
symbol ⟂ can be removed only in state q But on empty tape, 
we can not reach to state q from state s. 
Method 2: 
Note that to empty our stack, the stack bottom symbol ⟂ can 
be removed only in state q. To reach state q, from s or from 
p, we need symbol A on Top-of-the-stack (TOS). Symbol A 
is pushed in the stack by symbol a in the input string. So, 
our input string must have at least one a. 
In the initial state s, for every a in the input string, we push 
one A in the stack. Now, for every b in the input string, we 
pop one A from the stack. When all the b′s are over in the 
input string, we can move to state q if our TOS is A, so, to 
empty our stack at the end of any input string w, we must 
have more a′s than b′s in w. In the state q we can empty the 
stack & w is accepted. 
Also, our PDA accepts a+strings.

Mutual Exclusion:  The code ensures that both 
processes P1 and P2 cannot be in their critical section 
at the same time, because one waits for S1 == S2 
while the other waits for S1 != S2, so their conditions 
never allow simultaneous entry. 
 Progress is not satisfied:  If, for example, P1 is not 
interested in entering the critical section but P2 wants 
to enter, P2 could be blocked indefinitely waiting for 
P1 to change S1 to match S2. Thus, a process not 
intending to enter the critical section can prevent 
another from entering, violating the progress 
property. 
 Summary: The algorithm achieves mutual 
exclusion, but does not guarantee progress.

theory-of-computation-topic-3-m3-q12.explanation:
 L1 and L2 are recursive (decidable) because the 
condition is bounded by a fixed number of steps (2016). 
In 2016 steps, a Turing machine can read at most the 
first 2016 symbols on its tape. Because the alphabet is 
finite, there are a finite number of possible string prefixes 
of this length. A decider can simulate the machine on all 
these combinations for exactly 2016 steps. Since both 
the number of strings and the number of steps are finite, 
the simulation is guaranteed to halt and give an answer. 
 L3 is not recursive (undecidable) because checking 
whether a Turing machine accepts the empty string (ϵ) 
is the classic Blank Tape Acceptance Problem. 
According to Rice's Theorem, any non-trivial property 
about the language a Turing machine accepts cannot be 
decided by a general algorithm.

Solution: 
In a 2's complement system, overflow occurs 
during addition if and only if two numbers 
with the same sign are added together, but the 
result has the opposite sign.  
The problem specifies the following notation: 
 𝒂𝒏−𝟏 and 𝒃𝒏−𝟏 : The sign bits (Most 
Significant Bits) of the two input numbers. 
 𝒄𝑛−1 : The sign bit (Most Significant Bit) of 
the resulting sum. 
An overflow happens under exactly two 
scenarios: 
1. Adding two negative numbers yields a 
positive result: Both input sign bits are 1 , 
but the output sign bit is 0 . 
Condition 1 = 𝑎𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑏𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑐𝑛−1 
2. Adding two positive numbers yields a 
negative result: Both input sign bits are 𝜃, but 
the output sign bit is 1 . 
Condition 2 = 𝑎𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑏𝑛−1 ⋅ 𝑐𝑛−1 
Combining both mutually exclusive 
scenarios using an OR operation gives the 
complete expression for the overflow flag: 
 Overflow = 𝑎𝑛−1𝑏𝑛−1𝑐𝑛−1 + 𝑎𝑛−1𝑏𝑛−1𝑐𝑛−1

Explanation: 
In a singly linked list (SLL), each node has only a 
pointer to the next node. If we are given a pointer 
to the node to delete, we still need to know its 
previous node to change the link (prev->next = 
node->next). Since there is no backward pointer, 
we must traverse the list from the head to find the 
previous node. In the worst case, this takes O(n) 
time. 
In a doubly linked list (DLL), each node has 
pointers to both next and previous nodes. So, if we 
are given the node to delete, we can directly 
access its previous node and adjust links (prev- 
>next and 
next->prev) without any traversal. This takes O(1) 
time.

computer-organization-and-architecture-t.explanation:
There are N accesses to cache. 
Out of these n are unique block addresses. 
Now, we need to find the number of misses. 
(Minimum n misses are guaranteed whatever be the 
access sequence due to n unique block addresses). 
We are given that between two consecutive accesses 
to the same block, there can be only k unique block 
addresses. So, for a block to get replaced we can 
assume that all the next k block addresses go to the 
same set (given cache is set-associative) which will 
be the worst case scenario (they may also go to a 
different set but then there is less chance of a 
replacement). Now, if associativity size ≥ k, and if 
we use LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement 
policy, we can guarantee that these k accesses won't 
throw out our previously accessed cache entry (for 
<!-- PAGE 516 -->
Computer Organization and Architecture 
that we need at least k accesses). So, this means 
we are at the best-cache scenario for cache 
replacement — out of N accesses we miss only n 
(which are unique and cannot be helped from 
getting missed and there is no block replacement 
in cache). So, the miss ratio is n/N.

Number of sets = cache size / size of a set 
Size of a set = block size × number of blocks in a set 
= 8 words × 4 (4-way set-associative) 
= 8 × 4 × 4 (since a word is 32 bits = 4 bytes) 
= 128 bytes 
So, number of sets = 16 KB / 128 B = 128 
Now, we can divide the physical address space 
equally between these 128 sets. 
So, the number of bytes each set can access = 4 GB 
/ 128 
= 32 MB 
= 32 / 4 = 8 M words = 1 M blocks (220 blocks) 
So, we need 20 tag bits to identify these 220 blocks.

S1 is needed at times 1 and 5, so its forbidden 
latency is 5 − 1 = 4. 
S2 is needed at times 2 and 4, so its forbidden 
latency is 4 − 2 = 2. 
So, forbidden latency = (2, 4, 0) (0 by default is 
forbidden) 
Allowed latency = (1, 3, 5) (any value more than 5 
also). 
Collision vector (4, 3, 2, 1, 0) = 10101 which is the 
initial state as well. 
From the initial state we can have a transition after 
“1” or “3” cycles and we reach new states with 
collision vectors (10101 >> 1 + 10101 = 11111) and 
(10101 >> 3 + 10101 = 10111) respectively. 
These 2 become states 2 and 3 respectively. For “5” 
cycles we come back to state 1 itself. 
From state 2 (11111), the new collision vector is 
11111. We can have a transition only when we see 
the first 0 from the right. So, here it happens on the 
5th cycle only which goes to the initial state. (Any 
transition after 5 or more cycles goes to the initial 
state as we have 5 time slices). 
From state 3 (10111), the new collision vector is 
10111. So, we can have a transition on 3, which will 
give (10111 >> 3 + 10101 = 10111) the third state 
itself. For 5, we get the initial state. Thus all the 
transitions are complete. 
State/Time 1 3 5 
1(10101) 2 3 1 
2(11111) - - 1 
3(10111) - 3 1 
So, the minimum length cycle is of length 3 either 
from 3-3 or from 1-3,3-1.

Solution: 
 To print the string in reverse using recursion: 
 We must first read a character. 
If it is not newline, call reverse() again. 
After returning from recursion, print the character. 
 This way printing happens while unwinding the 
recursion, giving reverse order. 
 So we need: 
 ?1 → read character and check for newline 
?2 → print that character 
 Correct condition: 
(c = getchar()) != '\n' 
Correct print statement: 
putchar(c);
